name: Castor oil lashes
lead: Castor oil on eyelashes is a folk beauty practice in which castor oil, pressed from the seeds of Ricinus communis, is brushed along the lash line, usually at night, in the belief that it makes lashes look longer, thicker and darker. It is a staple of social media beauty content and of looksmaxxing discussion of lashes and brows, largely because it is inexpensive, easy to find and part of a long tradition of using plant oils as emollients.[1][2]

The appearance chain people describe is straightforward: a conditioning oil coats and moisturizes the hairs, reduces brittleness and breakage, and gives a glossier, fuller look, while some users also expect improved growth. Reference summaries state that no high-quality clinical trial has shown castor oil to stimulate eyelash growth, and that thickening claims rest on user reports, while noting that coating of the strands could change how lashes look without changing how they grow.[2]
The prescription product approved for eyelash growth is bimatoprost (Latisse), which has been studied in clinical trials; castor oil has not been tested the same way.[2][3]
infobox: Ricinoleic acid, about 90% of fatty acids [1]

paras: Castor oil is a pale vegetable oil from castor seeds, which are 40 to 60 percent oil. About 90 percent of its fatty acids are ricinoleates, and ricinoleic acid is unusual because it carries a hydroxyl group that makes it more polar than most plant fatty acids.[1][5] The seeds contain the toxin ricin, which is denatured by heat during oil extraction and is not part of the oil.[1][5]

The oil has long been used medicinally, with laxative use recorded in the Ebers Papyrus from around 1550 BC, and it appears in cosmetics, creams and moisturizers.[5] Hydrogenated castor oil is a common ingredient in lipsticks and other personal care products.[5]

Eyelash length is largely genetic, with upper lashes typically 7 to 8 mm, and the number of follicles is fixed before birth.[4] Each lash cycles through growth, regression and rest phases, and shed lashes are replaced from the same follicles.[4] This is the background against which users judge any change after applying an oil.

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and beauty routines
paras: Practitioners typically use a clean spoolie or cotton swab to coat lashes and brows, often as a nightly routine, and share before-and-after photographs over weeks. Many pair it with growth serums, lash lifts or mascara. The practice spreads mainly through beauty videos and forum posts rather than clinical sources.[2]

Proponents describe castor oil as improving the moisture, circulation or strength of lashes and brows.[2] A reference summary reports that reviews find at most weak or indirect evidence for improved hair luster through coating of the strands, which could make lashes look glossier without changing growth.[2]

The compound ricinoleic acid has attracted interest because of its effect on prostaglandin pathways: prostaglandin analogues such as bimatoprost are the basis of approved lash-growth treatment, and ricinoleic acid's effect on prostaglandin D2 has been studied in the context of scalp hair loss. The same summary states this has not been demonstrated for eyelashes.[2][3]

Topical castor oil is generally considered low-risk, and the Cosmetic Ingredient Review has deemed it safe in leave-on products, though rare contact dermatitis has been reported, particularly with undiluted use.[2] A reference summary advises that non-sterile castor oil should not be put in the eyes because of risks of irritation, infection and corneal damage.[2]

The castor seed allergen CB1A may affect people with hypersensitivity; Wikipedia says it is not present in the oil.[5] Reference works also say castor oil should not be ingested or used topically by pregnant women before term, and that no data exist on toxicity for nursing mothers.[5]

No studies found. A 2021 randomized trial of castor oil applied to the eyelids tested it for blepharitis, not lash growth, and reported improved eyelid signs without adverse events.[2] Separately, bimatoprost, the approved prostaglandin-analogue product, has its own trial record for lash growth.[3]

Castor oil is sold in drugstores and online in many forms, including cold-pressed and Jamaican black castor oil, and in pre-packaged lash and brow serums that add other ingredients. Social media content on lash growth routines made it a recurring beauty trend.[2]

timeline.event: Ebers Papyrus records castor oil as a laxative, one of its earliest documented uses.[5]
Randomized trial of castor oil on eyelids for blepharitis reports improved eyelid signs.[2]

lore.intro: Castor oil for lashes circulates in beauty and looksmaxxing discussion as a cheap alternative to prescription lash serums.[2]

claims.claim: Castor oil grows longer, thicker lashes
claims.believers: Users report fuller-looking lashes and brows after weeks of nightly use and credit the oil's moisture and ricinoleic acid content.[2]
claims.experts: A reference summary states that no high-quality clinical trial shows castor oil stimulates eyelash growth.[2] Eyelash follicle number is fixed before birth.[4]

claims.claim: The oil makes lashes look glossier and stronger
claims.believers: Proponents say coating the hairs reduces dryness and breakage so lashes look healthier.[2]
claims.experts: Reviews described in the reference summary report at most weak or indirect evidence for improved hair luster through coating.[2]

claims.claim: Ricinoleic acid acts like lash-growth drugs
claims.believers: Some users point to the oil's effect on prostaglandin pathways as a reason it should work like bimatoprost.[2]
claims.experts: The ricinoleic acid-prostaglandin D2 link has been studied for scalp hair loss and has not been demonstrated for eyelashes; bimatoprost is the approved lash-growth product.[2][3]

card.summary: Folk habit of oiling the lash line for longer lashes; popular online, with no trial showing it grows lashes.
card.note: Non-sterile oil should not get in the eyes; rare contact allergy.

quick.overview:
Castor oil is brushed on the lashes by people hoping for length and thickness. It is cheap and widely promoted on social media.

No clinical trial has shown it increases lash growth. Sources say any visible effect would more likely be a glossier, conditioned look, and the only product approved for lash growth in the sources is bimatoprost.
quick.mechanism: Proponents credit moisture and improved follicle circulation. No mechanism for lash growth has been demonstrated; related work on ricinoleic acid concerns scalp hair loss.
quick.risks: Generally low-risk topically, with rare contact dermatitis reported. Summaries note that non-sterile castor oil in the eyes can cause irritation, infection or corneal damage.

chain: Oil is brushed onto the lash line
Strands are coated and conditioned, reducing dryness and breakage
Lashes look glossier and fuller; users hope for added length
angle.text: People apply castor oil to lashes and sometimes brows hoping for longer, thicker hair. The conditioning effect on the hair shaft is the most commonly described visible change; growth effects are claimed by users.
